title: The designer's new skill: knowing how to say exactly what you want
description: AI executes fast, ambiguity included. Why writing criteria and intent has become one of the core skills of a Product Designer.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI inside a CRM, with the designer defining context, limits and criteria.

blocks.text: There's a skill that has always been part of a good designer's work:
knowing how to explain an idea.
To a developer.
To a PM.
To a stakeholder.
To a user.
To another designer.
Now we have to explain it to an AI.
And there's an important difference.
AI can execute very fast.
So any ambiguity can also be executed very fast.
Before, a vague idea had to go through several steps

data.idea: I think this screen could be better.
data.beforeNote: There were several moments to notice the idea still wasn't clear.

risk: We can start producing before we understand.

blocks.text: Speed changes the cost of ambiguity

lines: When creating something was expensive, thinking first was almost mandatory.
We can generate five interfaces in a few minutes.
But it raises a new question:
data.question: how many of those interfaces did we actually need to create?
after: The designer can end up spending more time evaluating possibilities than building the solution.
That's why the skill isn't simply knowing how to generate.

blocks.text: Precision doesn't mean controlling everything
A good prompt doesn't need to tell the AI exactly where every button goes.
Precision means defining what really matters.
For example:
Goal
Increase activation on first use.
User
Someone who just created an account.
Problem
The user doesn't understand which action to take first.
Behavior
The system should point to a clear next action.
Constraints
Don't add a new mandatory step.
Criterion
The user should be able to identify the next step without extra explanation.
That's much more useful than simply:
Make the onboarding more intuitive.
The designer needs to learn to write criteria

criteria: Make it so the user can find the main filter in under five seconds.
Make it so the error state explains what happened and what action can be taken.
Make it so the table can be understood without opening each row.
Make it so the main CTA has visual priority over secondary actions.
close: These instructions are much closer to product design.
Because they describe behavior and intent.

blocks.caption: Criteria describe behavior and intent, and give you something concrete to evaluate the result against.

blocks.text: A prompt is a way of thinking
Learning to write good prompts shouldn't mean memorizing formulas.
It should mean learning to:
In other words, many things that are already part of Product Design work.
AI doesn't eliminate these skills.
In some cases, it makes them even more visible.
Because now the distance between an idea and a solution has shrunk a lot.
And when production gets faster, the quality of the decision shows even more.
Maybe the future isn't about using AI better
Maybe it's about knowing better what to ask it for.
That difference seems small.
But it changes the designer's role quite a bit.
Before, a good idea had to be translated into a tool.
Now, the tool can produce from the idea.

lines: The problem is that a vague idea is still vague.
AI can turn an intent into an interface.
But we still need to know which intent is worth turning into an interface.
And maybe that's one of the Product Designer's new differentiators:

blocks.caption: Intent takes shape at each step, and evaluation loops back to the problem. A prompt is one step of thinking, not the end.
